fails.summary: Core toxicity direction is CORRECT and authoritatively confirmed: ASPCA classifies Mint (Mentha sp., Lamiaceae) as toxic to cats with toxic principle 'essential oils,' and clinical signs 'vomiting and diarrhea with large ingestions.' Compound (menthol/pulegone), mechanism (cats' limited hepatic metabolism of essential oils), family, and scientific name all check out. So there is NO safe-vs-toxic disagreement. However overall_factual=FAIL because of a REFUTED core severity claim driven by cross-contamination: the entry grades 'liver damage/failure' as 'fatal' for Common Garden Mint, but liver failure is the signature of PENNYROYAL (Mentha pulegium / pulegone) — a different species — or of highly concentrated oils, not fresh garden mint leaf. ASPCA attributes only vomiting/diarrhea to the plant. The entry repeatedly conflates fresh garden-mint leaf with concentrated essential oils, importing pennyroyal-specific liver toxicity and oil-specific respiratory distress / aspiration pneumonia / dermatitis as if they were garden-mint-leaf symptoms, and grading them severe-to-fatal. Several symptom 'notes' fields also contain corrupted/garbled trailing text and stray citation markers (e.g. 'Nausea and Excessive Drooling', '....Skin Irritation', '12', '24'), a content-quality defect. Recommended fix: re-scope severity to mild/moderate GI for leaf ingestion, clearly separate concentrated essential-oil risk, remove or relabel the pennyroyal-derived 'fatal' liver-failure symptom (or split pennyroyal into its own entry), and clean the garbled notes. The entry's educational content (lactose-intolerance mechanism, lactase deficiency after weaning, diarrhea/bloating/vomiting symptoms, 8-12 hour onset, and the 'not toxic but avoid' framing) is accurate and well-supported by ASPCA and VCA. However the structured severity field is wrong and dangerous: severity is set to 'toxic' while ASPCA explicitly classifies milk/dairy as NON-toxic, and the entry's own description text correctly says 'not toxic.' This internal safe-vs-toxic field-level contradiction is a false-alarm overstatement (safe_toxic_disagreement=true) and forces overall FAIL. Additional defects: toxicParts contains plant-anatomy terms ('Seed','Pit','Skin') cross-contaminated from a fruit/plant profile, which are meaningless for dairy (REFUTED); and the Pancreatitis symptom is graded 'severe' as a direct dairy effect when the fat-to-pancreatitis causal link is unproven in cats (established in dogs only) — UNVERIFIABLE/overstated. Recommended fixes: change severity to a non-toxic/caution grade to match ASPCA and the entry's own text; remove Seed/Pit/Skin from toxicParts; soften the pancreatitis claim to reflect feline-specific uncertainty.

This entry is a botanically incoherent CONFLATION of two different plants in two different families, and the named toxic compound is wrong. The slug and scientificName say "Nandina Photina spp." (mashing together Nandina, family Berberidaceae, with Photinia, family Rosaceae); the display name and entire description are about Photinia ("Photina/Photinia Red Leaf"); the declared family is "Rosaceae" (Photinia's family, NOT Nandina's). The symptom toxicology (cyanide, cherry-red mucous membranes, etc.) is generic cyanogenic-glycoside material. CORE REFUTATIONS: (1) Compound — entry claims the cyanogenic glycoside is "prunasin." ASPCA and peer-reviewed phytochemistry identify Nandina's cyanogenic glycosides as nandinin / p-glucosyloxymandelonitrile (plus protoberberine alkaloids); prunasin is the cyanogenic glycoside of Prunus species, not Nandina. REFUTED. (2) Family — entry says "Rosaceae"; ASPCA lists Nandina as Berberidaceae. REFUTED. (3) Identity — "Nandina Photina spp." is not a valid taxon; Nandina and Photinia are distinct genera. The directionally-correct fact (this is a cyanogenic-glycoside plant, toxic to cats, causing the cyanide cascade) holds for Nandina via ASPCA, so there is no safe<->toxic flip — but the entry as written cannot be trusted: it is cross-contaminated, mislabels the family, and names the wrong compound. Severity ("toxic") is defensible for Nandina but the symptom list overstates the typical real-world picture (ASPCA-listed signs are weakness/incoordination/seizures/coma/respiratory failure with death RARE in pets; entry escalates to "fatal," "sudden death frequently occurs"). Symptom "notes" fields also contain leaked draft artifacts (stray footnote markers like "2", "23", truncated sentences, embedded section headers "2. Respiratory Distress", "3. Mucous Membrane Discoloration"), indicating copy-paste contamination. overall_factual=FAIL due to REFUTED core compound and REFUTED family, plus the plant-identity conflation. Needs a decision: split into separate Nandina (Berberidaceae) and Photinia (Rosaceae) entries, fix the compound to nandinin for Nandina, and re-derive symptoms/severity from ASPCA. Note Photinia itself is NOT in the ASPCA cat database — its toxicity to cats is UNVERIFIABLE by authoritative sources (Merck covers horses/ruminants only).

Peanuts are correctly classified as NON-toxic to cats by the ASPCA (no cat-specific poison), so the core safe/toxic axis is right and there is no safe<->toxic disagreement. However the entry FAILS due to a REFUTED core mechanism: the xylitol "Hypoglycemia and Liver Failure" symptom is graded "fatal" for cats, but the Merck Veterinary Manual states plainly that "cats are not at risk for hypoglycemia or liver injury from xylitol toxicosis" and ASPCA APCC reports no known xylitol toxicity in cats. The entry's own notes even concede cats are "more resistant," yet it still grades the symptom fatal -- an overstatement of a wrong-species mechanism. Additional serious problems: (1) toxicParts "Stem, Root, Skin", scientificName "Peanuts", and family "Various" are nonsensical/cross-contaminated fields imported from a plant-profile template -- peanuts are a legume SEED (Arachis hypogaea, Fabaceae) eaten as food, not a plant whose stem/root are the hazard; (2) severity inflation -- four of six symptoms graded "fatal" (xylitol, sodium, aflatoxin, allergy) for an item the entry itself and ASPCA call non-toxic, which misrepresents risk from realistic exposures; (3) the "Severe Allergic Reaction / fatal anaphylaxis" symptom is unsupported by any authoritative veterinary source for peanuts specifically (anaphylaxis to foods is real but rare and peanut-specific feline cases are not documented). The genuine, well-supported risks are pancreatitis/GI upset from high fat, aflatoxin liver damage from moldy peanuts (FDA/Merck confirm aflatoxin affects pets/peanuts), and sodium ion toxicosis from heavily salted product (Pet Poison Helpline/Merck confirm salt toxicosis in cats). Recommend: change overall severity off "toxic" to a caution/non-toxic-with-risks grade, fix the plant-template metadata fields, and downgrade the xylitol and allergy symptoms.

DANGEROUS MISS. The entry sets severity="safe", but both the ASPCA toxic-plant database and Pet Poison Helpline classify peony (Paeonia officinalis) as TOXIC to cats. This is an internal contradiction too: the entry's own description and safetyNotes call it "mildly toxic," yet the machine-readable severity field is "safe." A user filtering for safe plants would be misled. The toxic compound (paeonol), family (Paeoniaceae), and core symptoms (vomiting, diarrhea, depression) all match ASPCA. However the entry adds a second compound, paeoniflorin, and a "CNS effects" mechanism that authoritative sources do not support, and its toxicParts/"highest in roots" claim conflicts with leads that point to bark; ASPCA does not enumerate parts. Severity is best described as mild-but-real GI toxicity, not "safe." overall_factual=FAIL on the safe-vs-toxic disagreement. Fix: set severity to a toxic/mild-toxic grade and reconcile the toxicParts and compound claims with authority.

FAIL. The persimmons entry has multiple core errors. (1) Severity='toxic' is a FALSE ALARM: persimmon is not on the ASPCA toxic list and all vet-reviewed sources call the ripe flesh non-toxic/safe in small amounts — the entry's own text even says 'not highly toxic.' (2) The cyanogenic/cyanide seed claim is REFUTED with wrong compound + fabricated mechanism — a classic cross-contamination from apple/cherry/peach stone-fruit pit profiles; the real seed danger is purely mechanical (choking/GI blockage). (3) toxicParts wrongly lists Flesh and Fruit as toxic when authorities say the flesh is the SAFEST part. (4) The symptoms array is corrupted: entry #1 is a truncated sentence fragment masquerading as a symptom, and 'Intestinal Obstruction' is over-graded 'fatal' with truncated notes. (5) scientificName ('Persimmons') and family ('Various') are placeholder/incorrect — should be Diospyros, Ebenaceae. CONFIRMED claims (genuine, mechanical/tannin risks): seed obstruction risk and unripe-fruit tannin GI irritation. Recommend: reclassify to low/conditional severity, delete the cyanide claim, remove Flesh/Fruit from toxicParts, rebuild the symptoms array, and fix taxonomy. safe_toxic_disagreement=true (false alarm: marked toxic but authorities deem flesh non-toxic).

Pine (Pinus spp., Pinaceae) entry is partly accurate on physical/GI hazards but has two serious errors. (1) Severity is marked "toxic," but ASPCA classifies pines (e.g. Blackjack/Ponderosa Pine, Pinaceae) as NON-TOXIC to cats — its only toxic principle, isocupressic acid, affects cattle, not cats. Pet Poison Helpline and VCA do flag genuine but MILD hazards (pine-oil GI irritation, needle obstruction/perforation), so the plant sits in a gray zone; the flat "toxic" grade contradicts ASPCA and overstates the plant's intrinsic toxicity (false-alarm direction). safe_toxic_disagreement=true. (2) The "Liver damage / FATAL" symptom is REFUTED for the pine tree: no authoritative source attributes hepatic toxicity to ingesting pine needles/sap; PPH's Christmas-tree article makes no mention of liver damage. Hepatotoxicity is a property of concentrated pine ESSENTIAL OIL (phenols/terpenes + cats' UGT deficiency), and the entry's own note concedes live-tree oil concentrations are low and not expected to cause major toxicity — so grading liver damage "fatal" for the tree is a mechanism/severity error. Additionally, the safetyNote claiming "Norfolk Island Pine (Araucaria) is considered more toxic to cats" is REFUTED: ASPCA lists Araucaria heterophylla (Norfolk Island / Australian Pine, family Araucariaceae) as NON-TOXIC to cats. Confirmed claims: identity/family, terpene/alpha-pinene GI-irritant mechanism, physical needle hazard, drooling/vomiting (mild), digestive blockage (severe), toxic parts (sap, needles). overall_factual=FAIL due to the refuted core liver-damage symptom and the safe↔toxic disagreement.

FAIL. Core safe-vs-toxic disagreement: the entry's machine-readable severity='toxic', but ASPCA explicitly classifies pistachios as NON-toxic to animals (risks are pancreatitis from large quantities and shell obstruction, not toxicity). The entry even contradicts itself — its own description and safetyNotes say 'not acutely toxic / no cat-specific compound,' which is correct, while the severity field overstates it as toxic (false alarm). Confirmed claims: fat -> GI upset/pancreatitis (ASPCA), and moldy nuts -> tremorgenic mycotoxins -> tremors/seizures with cats at risk (Pet Poison Helpline). Problems beyond severity: (1) the salted-pistachio 'Renal Stress, severity severe' symptom mislabels the mechanism (salt toxicosis is neurologic/electrolyte, not a severe chronic renal syndrome) and is unverifiable/overstated; (2) toxicParts include a nonsensical 'Stem' (cross-contamination from a plant template) while the genuinely dangerous SHELL (obstruction per ASPCA) is omitted; (3) the symptoms array contains a corrupted sentence-fragment 'symptom' and a truncated notes field, indicating data corruption; (4) scientificName/family are wrong placeholders (correct: Pistacia vera, Anacardiaceae). Recommend reclassifying severity to a 'caution/unsafe-but-not-toxic' tier, fixing the symptom array, adding shell-obstruction risk, and correcting toxicParts and taxonomy.

Core toxicity is correct: poppy (Papaver spp.) IS toxic to cats — confirmed by Pet Poison Helpline (any part ingested causes GI upset + CNS effects: inappetence, sedation, ataxia, coma). Compound class (isoquinoline alkaloids; opioid types in opium poppy, non-opioid in ornamentals) and the mu-opioid/CNS-depression mechanism are confirmed. The description and symptoms list correctly state DILATED pupils, which matches the established feline-specific response (opioids cause mydriasis in cats, unlike the miosis seen in dogs/humans). HOWEVER, overall_factual=FAIL because the safetyNotes contain a REFUTED, internally-contradictory, and clinically dangerous claim: 'pin-point pupils.' In cats, opioids produce DILATED pupils (mydriasis), not pin-point pupils (miosis); pin-point pupils is the human/dog presentation and is wrong for cats. The same entry lists 'Dilated pupils' as a symptom, so the document contradicts itself and the safetyNotes side is the incorrect one — a classic species cross-contamination error. No safe↔toxic disagreement (item is correctly toxic). Additional non-toxicology data defects: all four symptoms are mislabeled body_system='Gastrointestinal' (dilated pupils/ataxia/collapse are neurologic/ocular), and the symptom notes contain garbled run-on text ('...mammals1. 2. Vomiting'). ASPCA's own plant-list entries (Oriental/Iceland Poppy) could not be retrieved cleanly (nav shells only), so ASPCA confirmation is UNVERIFIABLE, but Pet Poison Helpline (priority 2) plus vet literature suffice to confirm the core toxicity.

Entry's overall direction (potato chips are unsafe for cats — high salt, plus hidden onion/garlic powder in flavored varieties) is correct, so there is no safe-vs-toxic disagreement. However it FAILS factual review on a core mechanism and on data integrity. (1) The "Acute Pancreatitis" symptom and the safetyNote claim that fat "can trigger pancreatitis" are REFUTED for cats: VCA states explicitly that, unlike dogs, cats do NOT appear to develop pancreatitis from high-fat diets — a classic dog-profile cross-contamination error, and it is graded "severe." (2) Severe data-corruption: the first symptom name is a truncated sentence fragment ("While the base ingredient of potato chips") with no clinical content — a fabricated/garbage symptom; multiple notes fields are truncated mid-word. (3) Severity overstatement: salt toxicity and solanine are labeled "fatal" though Pet Poison Helpline rates salt only moderate-to-severe and the snack-food dose realistically falls well short of fatal. (4) Plant-profile artifacts wrongly applied to a manufactured snack: scientificName "Potato chips", family "Various", and toxicParts (Skin, Peel, Cooked form, Raw form) are nonsensical for a processed food. CONFIRMED claims: sodium/salt toxicity and its symptoms (PPH, Merck); onion/garlic powder toxicity to feline red blood cells (ASPCA, Merck); solanine as the glycoalkaloid in green/unpeeled potatoes (Vetlexicon), with the entry correctly noting cooking/peeling removes most of it.

Pudding is a food (composite) entry, not a plant; family 'Various' and scientificName 'Pudding' are placeholders, acceptable for a manufactured food. Core toxicity claims that are real (chocolate/theobromine + caffeine methylxanthines; adult-cat lactose intolerance) are CONFIRMED by ASPCA and Merck, so the overall 'toxic' severity for pudding-as-eaten is defensible. HOWEVER the entry FAILS due to a dangerous safe-toxic disagreement: its safetyNotes assert 'Sugar-free pudding: xylitol — highly toxic to cats, causing dangerous hypoglycaemia.' This is REFUTED — ASPCA, Merck, and a peer-reviewed cat study (PubMed 29430681) all establish cats are NOT affected by xylitol (no hypoglycemia, no liver injury). Worse, the safetyNote directly contradicts the entry's own symptoms section, which correctly states cats are naturally resistant. The user-facing safetyNote spreads false toxicology. Additional defects: (1) a fabricated/garbage symptom entry literally named 'Because pudding is a manufactured dessert' (truncated artifact, no clinical content); (2) pancreatitis-from-pudding in cats is UNVERIFIABLE and severity 'severe' likely overstated; (3) several symptom 'notes' contain truncated text and stray footnote markers (e.g., 'Darker chocolate puddings are significantly', 'cats do not suffer this dangerous h'), indicating copy-paste/scraping contamination. Recommend: correct the xylitol safetyNote to state cats are not affected by xylitol (keep the chocolate warning as the genuine danger), delete the malformed symptom, and clean truncated notes.

The entry merges two botanically distinct Asteraceae plants into one — Ragwort/Tansy Ragwort (Senecio jacobaea) and Common Tansy (Tanacetum vulgare). Both ARE independently listed as toxic to cats by the ASPCA, so there is no safe/toxic disagreement. However, the entry commits a serious compound/mechanism error by attributing pyrrolizidine alkaloids (jacobine, retrorsine, etc.) to BOTH plants. Pyrrolizidine alkaloids and the PA->reactive-pyrrole->DNA-crosslink hepatotoxic mechanism belong ONLY to Senecio. Tanacetum vulgare's toxins are thujone and sesquiterpene lactones — NOT pyrrolizidine alkaloids. The entry then cross-contaminates in the opposite direction: its single "Liver damage" symptom note attributes the damage to "a volatile oil containing thujone" — a Tansy property — even though thujone is not a Senecio/ragwort compound and is not the PA hepatotoxic mechanism described elsewhere in the same record. This is the classic cross-contamination-from-another-plant failure mode operating in both directions within one entry. Additionally, "senecioline" is not a recognized pyrrolizidine alkaloid in the authoritative literature (Merck names seneciphylline, retrorsine, monocrotaline, jacobine); it appears fabricated or misspelled. overall_factual = FAIL because a core compound claim (PAs in Tansy) is REFUTED and the symptom-note mechanism is cross-contaminated. The toxic-to-cats grading and severity are correct, and the Senecio PA mechanism is accurately described.

Core toxicology is sound and confirmed by authoritative sources: raw yeast dough is genuinely toxic to cats via two confirmed mechanisms (CO2 fermentation -> gastric distension/bloat/diaphragm compression, and ethanol fermentation -> CNS and respiratory depression). Every listed symptom (abdominal distension, vomiting, ataxia, disorientation, weakness, hypothermia, hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, seizures, coma, respiratory distress) is corroborated by the Merck Veterinary Manual and/or Pet Poison Helpline. Severity grading (toxic/medical emergency, multiple fatal-graded signs) is appropriate and not overstated. No safe<->toxic disagreement.\n\nTwo defects drive the FAIL verdict: (1) toxicParts is cross-contaminated from a fruit/plant profile -- it lists \"Seed\", \"Pit\", \"Skin\", which are meaningless for dough (the explicitly flagged cross-contamination failure mode); (2) the mechanism claim that cats \"lack the specific enzymes\" / \"lack alcohol dehydrogenase\" is REFUTED as worded -- peer-reviewed feline ADH work (AVMA J 2000, PubMed 10772113) shows cats HAVE alcohol dehydrogenase but at ~2-fold reduced capacity. The clinical conclusion (cats are especially sensitive to ethanol) is correct, so this is an overstatement of a correct directional claim, but it should be reworded to \"limited/reduced capacity to metabolize alcohol.\" Also flagged: scientificName \"Raw dough\" and family \"Various\" are non-meaningful placeholders for a food entry (should be null). Recommended fixes: clear/correct toxicParts, reword the ADH claim, null out scientificName/family.

Core toxic/non-toxic status is CORRECT: ASPCA lists Strelitzia reginae (Strelitziaceae) as toxic to cats, so no safe-vs-toxic disagreement. However the entry's MECHANISM and several SYMPTOMS are REFUTED, which fails the entry. ASPCA states the toxic principle is simply "GI irritants" with clinical signs "mild nausea, vomiting, drowsiness; caused mainly by fruit and seeds." The entry instead claims the active compounds are TANNINS and HYDROCYANIC ACID / cyanide-releasing cyanogenic glycosides — neither is supported by ASPCA or Pet Poison Helpline; these appear only on SEO/blog content. Built on that false cyanide mechanism, the entry adds a fabricated/over-stated symptom "Labored Breathing (Respiratory Distress)" attributed to cyanide in the leaves, and an unsupported "Eye Discharge" symptom (note falsely claims it is "noted in multiple veterinary sources"). ASPCA pins toxicity mainly to fruit/seeds, whereas the entry attributes systemic respiratory toxicity to leaves. Severity grade "cautious"/mild GI is reasonable and matches ASPCA, but the cyanide-poisoning framing materially overstates the hazard. Two symptom notes also contain corrupted concatenated text ("...irritants.Labored Breathing", "...prussic acid).Eye Discharge", "...sources.Drowsiness") indicating data-quality defects. Recommend: replace compound/mechanism with "GI irritants," remove Labored Breathing and Eye Discharge, narrow toxic parts toward fruit/seeds per ASPCA.

CRITICAL: The entry's structured severity field is "safe" while ASPCA classifies the Tradescantia genus (listed as T. fluminensis "Inch Plant," same genus/family Commelinaceae as T. spathacea) as TOXIC to cats. This is a dangerous safe-marked-but-toxic miss (safe_toxic_disagreement=true). The field also contradicts the entry's own description, which calls the plant "mildly toxic." Beyond the severity error, the core mechanism is misstated: ASPCA's documented clinical sign for Tradescantia is DERMATITIS (contact/sap irritation), and ASPCA does NOT list Tradescantia among its calcium-oxalate plants (those are Araceae — Dieffenbachia, Philodendron). The entry's claim that calcium oxalate crystals cause mechanical oral/GI irritation appears to be cross-contamination from an aroid profile and is REFUTED/unsupported by the top authority. The dermatitis symptom and family (Commelinaceae) are CONFIRMED. GI symptoms (drooling/vomiting/diarrhea) appear only in lower-tier sources, not in ASPCA's clinical-sign listing, so they are UNVERIFIABLE against authority. overall_factual=FAIL on both the safe-vs-toxic disagreement and the refuted core mechanism.

CRITICAL FALSE ALARM. The entry grades Prairie Lily (Zephyranthes drummondii) as toxic ("severity": "cautious", isToxic implied) and describes a lycorine-driven emetic/hypotensive/CNS syndrome with vomiting, diarrhea, drooling, tremors, hypotension, and convulsions. The authoritative ASPCA Animal Poison Control plant database lists this exact species — Prairie Lily, Zephyranthes drummondii, family Amaryllidaceae, common names giant rain lily / hill country rain lily — as NON-TOXIC to both cats and dogs, with no toxic principle assigned. This is lethal failure mode (a): an item ASPCA calls non-toxic is marked toxic. The toxicology described (lycorine, phenanthridine alkaloids, bulb-most-concentrated, emetic-center activation, vasodilation/hypotension, CNS depression, convulsions) is the classic profile of Amaryllidaceae bulb plants such as daffodil (Narcissus) and amaryllis (Hippeastrum) — a cross-contamination from a different plant's profile (the dataset's noted common error). While the genus Zephyranthes does botanically contain lycorine and the family attribution is correct, no authority confirms clinical toxicity for THIS species in cats; ASPCA explicitly clears it. The species-specific ASPCA entry overrides generic "less toxic lily / GI upset" roundup mentions, which stem from Lilium-name confusion. Recommend: reclassify as non-toxic per ASPCA, or remove the entry. The discrete symptoms, mechanism, and severity are all unsupported for this plant.

verify.summary: Pennyroyal (Mentha pulegium) entry is factually sound on all core toxicity claims. It is correctly graded as toxic to cats; the named compound (pulegone, bioactivated to menthofuran), the mechanism (direct hepatocellular necrosis / glutathione depletion), and the symptom set (vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, tremors/seizures, lethargy, collapse, respiratory distress) are all corroborated by authoritative/clinical sources (ASPCA dedicated pennyroyal page, PetMD, Pet Poison Helpline, VIN clinical literature). Family Lamiaceae confirmed. One non-core content error: toxicParts lists only Root/Stem/Flower, omitting leaves and the whole aerial plant where the pulegone-bearing volatile oil is actually concentrated. Also: the symptoms[].notes fields contain garbled, leaked source artifacts (e.g. "...lead to death1.... 2. Seizures and Neurological Impairment", stray citation digits) — a data-hygiene defect, not a factual error. Neither issue flips the safe/toxic verdict, so overall PASS, but toxicParts and the notes should be corrected.

claim_verdicts.claim: Primary toxic compound is pulegone.
claim_verdicts.note: PetMD states the active poison is pulegone, hepatotoxic and causing severe liver damage; corroborated across sources.

claim_verdicts.claim: Pulegone is metabolised to menthofuran in the liver, the true hepatotoxic agent.
claim_verdicts.note: Veterinary clinical literature (VIN) states pulegone is bioactivated to the hepatotoxic metabolite menthofuran, causing direct hepatic necrosis.
claim_verdicts.authority: VIN (Atlantic Coast Veterinary Conference clinical proceedings)

claim_verdicts.claim: Mechanism: direct hepatocellular necrosis amplified by glutathione depletion.
claim_verdicts.note: Clinical sources describe direct hepatocyte injury/hepatic necrosis and coagulopathy; reactive metabolite depletes glutathione. Glutathione-depletion detail is mechanistically standard for pulegone/menthofuran and consistent with cited toxicology.

claim_verdicts.claim: Symptoms include vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy/listlessness.
claim_verdicts.note: PetMD symptom list includes listlessness, vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy.

claim_verdicts.claim: Severe cases cause acute liver failure with jaundice.
claim_verdicts.note: Liver failure is the central outcome; jaundice is not in PetMD's bullet list but is named by Pet Poison Helpline-aligned veterinary sources and is the expected clinical sign of acute hepatic failure. Not fabricated.
claim_verdicts.authority: Pet Poison Helpline / veterinary clinical sources

claim_verdicts.claim: Symptoms include seizures and tremors / neurological signs.
claim_verdicts.note: PetMD lists seizures and coma; case literature describes seizures preceding death.

claim_verdicts.claim: Symptoms include difficulty breathing / respiratory distress (and coughing, sneezing).
claim_verdicts.note: PetMD lists difficulty breathing, coughing up blood, bloody nose. Respiratory distress confirmed; specific 'sneezing' is not separately attested but is minor and within the respiratory cluster.

claim_verdicts.claim: Pennyroyal essential oil is especially dangerous; topical/dermal application can cause fatal liver failure; historically misused as a flea treatment.
claim_verdicts.note: Case report: dog dermally exposed to pennyroyal oil (~2 g/kg) became listless within 1 hr, vomited within 2 hr, then diarrhea, hemoptysis, epistaxis, seizures, death. Sources confirm misuse as flea repellent.

claim_verdicts.claim: Plant family is Lamiaceae (mint family).
claim_verdicts.note: Mentha pulegium is a member of Lamiaceae; widely corroborated.

claim_verdicts.claim: Toxic parts are Root, Stem, and Flower (only).
claim_verdicts.note: Pulegone is in the volatile oil throughout the plant and is most concentrated in the leaves/aerial parts. Listing only root/stem/flower omits the leaves, the principal source of the toxin, and no authoritative source restricts toxicity to those three parts. Whole plant and its oil are toxic. This is a content error (likely a generic/templated toxic-parts fill), though it does not change the toxic verdict.
claim_verdicts.authority: Veterinary toxicology consensus (pulegone in volatile oil, concentrated in leaves)

claim_verdicts.claim: Scientific name Mentha spp. and common name garden/common mint
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA lists 'Mint' as Mentha sp., common names including garden mint, spearmint, peppermint.

claim_verdicts.claim: Plant family Lamiaceae
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA gives family Lamiaceae. Correct.

claim_verdicts.claim: Mint is toxic to cats (severity=toxic / isToxic=true)
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA explicitly classifies Mint as 'Toxic to Cats'. No safe/toxic disagreement; entry direction is correct.

claim_verdicts.claim: Toxic principle/compound is essential oils, specifically menthol and pulegone
claim_verdicts.authority: ASPCA Animal Poison Control; Pet Poison Helpline; VCA
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA gives toxic principle = 'Essential Oils.' Pet Poison Helpline/VCA confirm peppermint oil (menthol) and pennyroyal oil (pulegone) as toxic essential oils for cats. Mechanism (cats' limited hepatic metabolism of these compounds) is well supported.

claim_verdicts.claim: Symptoms of leaf ingestion: vomiting and diarrhea
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA clinical signs for Mint: 'Vomiting and diarrhea with large ingestions.' This is the ONLY symptom set ASPCA attributes to the plant.

claim_verdicts.claim: Symptom: drooling/hypersalivation, nausea, lethargy/weakness, loss of appetite
claim_verdicts.authority: VCA / Pet Poison Helpline (essential-oil context only)
claim_verdicts.note: Drooling and lethargy/weakness are documented for concentrated ESSENTIAL OIL exposure, not for fresh garden-mint leaf. ASPCA does not list them for the plant. Plausible for oil exposure but presented here as general mint symptoms; not confirmed by an authority for leaf ingestion.

claim_verdicts.claim: Symptom: contact dermatitis / skin irritation from the plant (severity mild)
claim_verdicts.note: No authoritative source attributes contact dermatitis to garden mint leaf in cats. VCA notes skin redness/burns from concentrated essential OIL, not the plant. Flagged: appears extrapolated.

claim_verdicts.claim: Symptom: respiratory distress, dyspnea, coughing, sneezing, aspiration pneumonia (severity severe)
claim_verdicts.authority: VCA / Pet Poison Helpline (essential-oil context only)
claim_verdicts.note: Difficulty breathing and aspiration risk are documented for concentrated/inhaled ESSENTIAL OILS, not for the garden-mint plant. Entry presents this as a primary mint risk; valid only for the oil. Severity grading 'severe' is for oil exposure, overstated for the plant itself.

claim_verdicts.claim: Symptom: liver damage/failure graded 'fatal' for Common Garden Mint
claim_verdicts.note: Liver failure is the hallmark of PENNYROYAL (Mentha pulegium) oil / pulegone, a DIFFERENT species, or of highly concentrated oils. ASPCA's clinical signs for plain Mint are only vomiting/diarrhea. Grading garden-mint-leaf ingestion as 'fatal' liver failure is cross-contamination from the pennyroyal profile and severity over-statement. Symptom list (vomiting/GI, lethargy/weakness, pale or icteric mucous membranes, tachypnea/dyspnea, tachycardia, hemoglobinuria, collapse/death) all map to Merck/ASPCA clinical signs. Two NON-toxicological data-quality flags: the scientificName field literally reads \"Onions\" instead of \"Allium cepa\" (the description body has it correct), and family is \"Various\" rather than ASPCA's Liliaceae/Amaryllidaceae. claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA names the toxic principle as N-propyl disulfide exactly; Merck describes sulfur-containing oxidants released by chopping/cooking/chewing. Compound naming is accurate.

claim_verdicts.note: Merck: toxins cause oxidative damage to RBCs leading to Heinz body formation and methemoglobinemia, then intravascular hemolysis/anemia. Mechanism correct.

Listing pulegone as a lead toxin misattributes pennyroyal's toxicology to orange mint.

claim_verdicts.note: Tremors and ataxia are documented for concentrated ESSENTIAL-OIL poisoning, not for ingesting the mint plant, for which ASPCA lists only vomiting/diarrhea. claim_verdicts.note: 'Difficulty breathing' is a documented essential-OIL sign, but ASPCA's mint PLANT entry lists no respiratory signs. claim_verdicts.note: 'Redness or burns on lips, gums, tongue, or skin' is a real sign of CONCENTRATED essential-oil contact, but not of contact with the living mint plant; ASPCA lists no dermal signs for mint. Cross-contaminated from the oil profile.

claim_verdicts.claim: toxicParts = Leaf, Entire Plant.
claim_verdicts.note: ASPCA does not enumerate toxic parts for mint; essential oils are present throughout aerial parts, so 'leaf/entire plant' is plausible but not authority-confirmed.

claim_verdicts.note: The symptom notes contain corrupted editorial scaffolding ('2. Neurological Impairment', '3. Respiratory Distress', '4. Liver Damage / Failure', '5. Dermal and Mucous Membrane Burns') and dangling citation numbers. These are fabrication/ingestion-error red flags and indicate the symptom list was machine-assembled from a generic essential-oil article, not curated for orange mint.

verify.summary: No safe-vs-toxic disagreement: ASPCA confirms Mint (Mentha sp., Lamiaceae) is toxic to cats, so the toxic grading and the Lamiaceae family are CORRECT, and the mechanism (cats' deficient UGT/glucuronidation of monoterpenes) is supported by Merck/VCA. The plant-level GI symptom profile in safetyNotes (mild, self-limiting vomiting/diarrhea/drooling) matches ASPCA. However the entry has serious quality/severity defects that warrant review rather than a pass: (1) Compound list is misleading — orange mint (Mentha citrata) oil is dominated by linalool and linalyl acetate; pulegone is at most a minor/variable constituent and is the hallmark toxin of PENNYROYAL, so listing it as a lead toxin misattributes pennyroyal toxicology. ASPCA's actual toxic principle is generically 'essential oils.' (2) The structured symptom array systematically OVERSTATES severity for a garden-plant entry: GI graded 'severe' (ASPCA = mild, large ingestions only), liver failure graded 'fatal' (ASPCA lists no hepatic sign for the plant), plus seizures, respiratory distress, and dermal burns — these are documented for CONCENTRATED essential-oil exposure (VCA), not for ingesting the living mint plant, and were cross-contaminated into the plant profile. (3) The symptom notes contain corrupted editorial scaffolding and dangling footnote digits ('2. Neurological Impairment', '3. Respiratory Distress', etc.), evidence the symptom list was machine-assembled from a generic essential-oil article. Net: core toxicity direction is correct, but compound emphasis is REFUTED and the per-symptom severities are overstated/unverifiable, so overall_factual = NEEDS_REVIEW. Recommend: replace pulegone-lead framing with linalool/linalyl-acetate + 'essential oils'; downgrade plant-ingestion symptoms to mild GI per ASPCA; clearly silo the severe neuro/respiratory/hepatic/dermal signs as concentrated-essential-oil-only; and strip the corrupted note artifacts.

Core toxicology is CONFIRMED against authoritative sources. ASPCA classifies Peach (Prunus persica, Rosaceae) as toxic to cats; toxic principle is cyanogenic glycosides (amygdalin) in stems, leaves, and seeds/pits, releasing cyanide. The entry's compound, mechanism (amygdalin -> beta-glucosidase -> HCN -> blocks cellular oxygen use), scientific name, and family all match ASPCA and Pet Poison Helpline. The 'cherry-red mucous membranes' sign matches ASPCA's 'brick red mucous membranes.' However the entry has two notable defects warranting review: (1) toxicParts wrongly lists 'Flesh' and 'Fruit' as toxic, which contradicts both ASPCA (flesh not cited as toxic) and the entry's own description ('flesh is safe for cats in small amounts') -- REFUTED. The entry merges two botanically distinct Asteraceae plants into one — Ragwort/Tansy Ragwort (Senecio jacobaea) and Common Tansy (Tanacetum vulgare). Both ARE independently listed as toxic to cats by the ASPCA, so there is no safe/toxic disagreement. However, the entry commits a serious compound/mechanism error by attributing pyrrolizidine alkaloids (jacobine, retrorsine, etc.) to BOTH plants. Pyrrolizidine alkaloids and the PA->reactive-pyrrole->DNA-crosslink hepatotoxic mechanism belong ONLY to Senecio. Tanacetum vulgare's toxins are thujone and sesquiterpene lactones — NOT pyrrolizidine alkaloids. The entry then cross-contaminates in the opposite direction: its single "Liver damage" symptom note attributes the damage to "a volatile oil containing thujone" — a Tansy property — even though thujone is not a Senecio/ragwort compound and is not the PA hepatotoxic mechanism described elsewhere in the same record. This is the classic cross-contamination-from-another-plant failure mode operating in both directions within one entry. Additionally, "senecioline" is not a recognized pyrrolizidine alkaloid in the authoritative literature (Merck names seneciphylline, retrorsine, monocrotaline, jacobine); it appears fabricated or misspelled. overall_factual = FAIL because a core compound claim (PAs in Tansy) is REFUTED and the symptom-note mechanism is cross-contaminated. The toxic-to-cats grading and severity are correct, and the Senecio PA mechanism is accurately described.

verify.summary: All core toxicology claims for the Calla Lily (Zantedeschia aethiopica) entry are CONFIRMED against authoritative sources. Compound (insoluble calcium oxalate crystals / raphides), mechanism (mechanical raphide injury to oral/GI soft tissues on chewing), and family (Araceae) match ASPCA and Pet Poison Helpline verbatim. Every listed symptom — oral pain/burning, hypersalivation, vomiting/anorexia, dysphagia, and rare severe laryngeal-edema dyspnea — is corroborated by ASPCA and PPH. The severity grading (toxic but markedly less dangerous than true lilies) and the 'imposter lily / no kidney failure' distinction are confirmed by UC Davis VetMed; only Lilium and Hemerocallis cause feline acute kidney injury. No safe↔toxic disagreement, no wrong compound/mechanism, no fabricated symptoms, no cross-contamination from a different plant's profile. Overall: PASS. One non-factual data-quality issue: the symptom 'notes' fields contain corrupted concatenated trailing text and a mid-word truncation ('...considered \"impos') — recommend editorial cleanup, but it does not affect factual accuracy.

CRITICAL FALSE ALARM. The entry grades Prairie Lily (Zephyranthes drummondii) as toxic ("severity": "cautious", isToxic implied) and describes a lycorine-driven emetic/hypotensive/CNS syndrome with vomiting, diarrhea, drooling, tremors, hypotension, and convulsions. The authoritative ASPCA Animal Poison Control plant database lists this exact species — Prairie Lily, Zephyranthes drummondii, family Amaryllidaceae, common names giant rain lily / hill country rain lily — as NON-TOXIC to both cats and dogs, with no toxic principle assigned. This is lethal failure mode (a): an item ASPCA calls non-toxic is marked toxic. The toxicology described (lycorine, phenanthridine alkaloids, bulb-most-concentrated, emetic-center activation, vasodilation/hypotension, CNS depression, convulsions) is the classic profile of Amaryllidaceae bulb plants such as daffodil (Narcissus) and amaryllis (Hippeastrum) — a cross-contamination from a different plant's profile (the dataset's noted common error). While the genus Zephyranthes does botanically contain lycorine and the family attribution is correct, no authority confirms clinical toxicity for THIS species in cats; ASPCA explicitly clears it. The species-specific ASPCA entry overrides generic "less toxic lily / GI upset" roundup mentions, which stem from Lilium-name confusion. Recommend: reclassify as non-toxic per ASPCA, or remove the entry. The discrete symptoms, mechanism, and severity are all unsupported for this plant.
